summary: Defines a Telnet option that lets one side tell the other to turn remote flow control on or off. Flow control is how a terminal user's software starts and stops the text flowing so the screen is not overwhelmed. It was replaced by RFC 1372.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1080 defines a Telnet option for remotely enabling or disabling flow control between a Telnet process and its terminal. It was later replaced by RFC 1372.

questions: how does telnet control flow of output
what does the telnet remote flow control option do
subtitle: A Telnet option for remotely turning terminal flow control on or off

tldr.problem: Software flow control uses input characters that some applications need to treat as ordinary data.
tldr.mechanism: After Telnet peers negotiate the option, one peer can send subcommands to enable or disable flow control in the other peer.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1080 defines Telnet option 33 and was later replaced by RFC 1372.

sections.title: Why Remote Flow Control Is Needed
sections.content:
This option lets a host control flow control for data sent from a Telnet process to its attached terminal. Software flow control commonly uses XOFF and XON characters in the same stream as ordinary input data.

Some host programs need users to be able to enter every possible ASCII character. Disabling software flow control lets those characters be read as input, so the RFC defines a way for the host to pass the flow-control state to the user Telnet process.
sections.plainLanguage: Some applications need characters that are normally reserved to pause or resume output. This option lets the host change that behavior without using those characters as commands.

sections.title: Negotiating the Option
sections.content:
The option is named TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL and has code 33. The peers first exchange WILL and DO to agree that one side can send flow-control commands. They must complete this negotiation before sending subnegotiations.

Once they agree, the sender of DO can command the other process. The sender of WILL must enable flow control as soon as the WILL and DO exchange completes, establishing a known starting state. Either side may turn off the option with WONT or DONT.
sections.plainLanguage: The two Telnet processes first agree to use the option. After that, one side can send commands to change flow control in the other side.

sections.title: Enable and Disable Commands
sections.content:
The OFF subcommand has code 0 and asks the receiver to disable flow control. The ON subcommand has code 1 and asks the receiver to enable it. Neither command carries additional data.

The RFC says that subnegotiation codes other than 0 and 1 should be ignored. It also warns that after the option is disabled, flow control may return to an implementation-defined default state.
sections.plainLanguage: Code 0 asks the other side to turn flow control off, and code 1 asks it to turn flow control on. Other command codes are ignored.
